# The Space Between Wonder and Wednesday

There is a particular kind of hunger that persists beneath the surface of an ordinary life—one that goes unnoticed by the calendar of weddings and doctor's appointments, the birthday parties and the divorce papers, the quiet accumulation of years that make up what we call a life. The narrator moves through these milestones as anyone does: getting married, undergoing medical procedures, attending parties full of familiar faces, eventually divorcing, becoming a parent. These are the events that mark time, that fill photo albums and small talk. But beneath this procession of the expected, something else is happening—a persistent, almost desperate searching for the magical, the transcendent, some sign that the world contains more than what can be measured or scheduled.

This search takes the form of a ritual of listening. The narrator holds shells to their ear, waiting for something beyond the ocean's static hum. They crouch beside dead birds on sidewalks, searching for some final message in stillness. They press their ear to flowers, to the folded silence of petals, hoping for a whisper. They stand in valleys, calling out, waiting for the land itself to answer with something more than an echo. Each attempt follows the same trajectory: anticipation, straining attention, and then—nothing. Or worse than nothing: an echo, a hollow return of the same voice that was sent out, the world reflecting back only what was given to it, refusing to add anything of its own.

This search occurs in the interstices of daily life, creating a strange double vision. While flossing teeth at the bathroom sink, the narrator might imagine a bird speaking in complete sentences. While waiting for brunch reservations, they might glimpse—or wish to glimpse—a yawning hole opening in the pavement, leading somewhere else entirely. While standing on a step stool changing a burnt-out bulb, they might catch sight of a purple panther slipping between the trees at the edge of the yard. These images don't integrate smoothly into the narrative of adult life; they jut out, strange and vivid, refusing to be assimilated into the beige continuity of chores and errands. This friction is the point: the ordinary and the miraculous do not coexist easily. They exist in tension, each one interrupting the other, each one insisting on its own reality.

Underlying this entire search is an implicit theory about where the magic went. The talking bird, we understand, belonged to childhood—perhaps literally, perhaps as a symbol for a way of perceiving the world that children possess and adults lose. Floorboards that once sang beneath small feet, creaking out something like music, something like language, have gone silent, or perhaps they never sang at all except in the retrospective glow of memory. This is the central wound of the piece: not that magic never existed, but that it existed once, in a specific and irretrievable past, and that growing up meant leaving it behind—not through a single dramatic break, but through the slow accretion of mundane obligations, one responsibility stacked on another until the singing floor was buried under adult life.

And so the narrator searches, not for something new, but for something lost—trying to recover a channel of communication that once seemed open, wanting to prove that the door hasn't been sealed shut for good. This is why the mundane events of adult life take on a subtle desperation: the marriage, the party, the medical procedure are not just things that happen, but also opportunities, however unlikely, for the extraordinary to break through. Perhaps at the wedding, something enchanted might occur. Perhaps in the hospital, waiting for results, some sign might present itself. Every ordinary moment holds the possibility, however faint, of transcendence.

But the piece does not end in triumph or discovery. It ends in resignation. The narrator's mission—unstated but understood throughout, the quiet quest to reconnect with a magical register of existence—comes to a close, not with fireworks, but with silence. The valleys stop offering even echoes. The shells reveal nothing but the sound of blood in one's own ear, mistaken for ocean. The world, it seems, has sealed itself, closing whatever door once stood ajar in childhood. The narrator is left not with an answer, but with the accumulated weight of ordinary years: flossing, brunches, changing light bulbs, all the tasks that make up an adult life, absent now of any hope that they might crack open into something else. What remains is not devastation, but a quiet acceptance—the recognition that some doors, once closed, do not reopen, and that the search itself, however long undertaken, has reached its natural, unglamorous end.

# What the Shell Never Said

When I was young—six, maybe seven—a bird spoke to me in my grandmother's garden. I have never doubted this. It said something like *wait* or *soon*, in a voice like wind moving through a keyhole, and then it was only a bird again, tilting its head at the seed I'd scattered. Around the same time, I found a hole in the earth behind the toolshed that seemed to breathe—a slow exhale of cool, mineral air, as if the ground itself were drowsy and vast. I told no one. I understood, even then, that these things belonged to a country adults had forgotten how to visit, and I did not want to be laughed out of it.

I carried that country with me the way you carry a key to a house you've moved out of. Useless, but you don't throw it away.

I married at twenty-six, in a small stone church that smelled of dust and lilies, and during the ceremony I pressed a shell I'd brought in secret to my ear, hoping it might offer some blessing more essential than the priest's. It gave me the ocean, or something like the ocean—a hollow roar that could have been anything, could have been my own blood insisting on itself. I told myself it was enough.

There was a career after that, unremarkable and steady, the kind that fills out a life the way sand fills a jar—not dramatically, but completely, until there is no room left to notice it happening. I sat in rooms with fluorescent light and said the things that needed saying. On lunch breaks I sometimes walked to a small park and stood before the flowerbeds, waiting, the way you wait for a friend who is late but who has never once, in your whole life together, failed to come. The flowers did what flowers do. They opened. They closed. I decided this was itself a kind of language, though I could never translate a single phrase.

Children came—two of them, a boy and a girl, loud and gorgeous and entirely uninterested in shells or holes in the ground. I took them to the mountains once, to a valley so wide and green it seemed to hold its breath, and I stood at its center and shouted, just to hear what would come back. What came back was my own voice, thinned and delayed, saying my own words in a stranger's timing. My daughter laughed and shouted her name into the valley too, delighted by the trick of it. I did not tell her I had been listening for something else.

The marriage ended the way most do—not with lightning, but with erosion, two people slowly becoming coastlines that no longer met. In the apartment I moved to afterward, I kept the shell on the windowsill. Some nights, unable to sleep, I picked it up like a phone I was hoping might finally ring with news. The ocean again. Only the ocean. Never once the small voice from the garden, never the cool breathing dark behind the shed.

I am older now. My children visit on holidays and speak to me in the practical language of the world—insurance, holidays, the price of gas—and I answer them in kind, because that conversation, too, deserves tending. But sometimes, walking at dusk past a hedge full of restless birds, I stop and wait, the way I waited at seven, at twenty-six, at forty, at the edge of that valley with my daughter's laughter still bright in the air.

The birds go on being birds. The ground, wherever I press my ear to it, is only ground—solid, indifferent, keeping whatever it keeps to itself. If there was ever a door, I think now it must have been a door made only for children, sized to a smallness I have long since grown out of, and it has closed so quietly behind me that I never heard the latch.

Still, most evenings, I find some shell, some flower, some hollow of stone or wind, and I put my ear against it anyway. Not because I expect an answer.

Because once, it answered, and a life is a long time to stop believing your own ears.

# The Cycle of Remove, Get, and Have

Life often moves in a rhythm of acquiring, letting go, and possessing. These three simple words—Remove, Get, and Have—capture a cycle that shapes how we manage our homes, our habits, and even our minds.

**Remove** is often the first step toward clarity. Whether it's clearing out a cluttered closet, deleting unused apps from a phone, or letting go of a toxic relationship, removal creates space. It's an act of subtraction that, paradoxically, often leads to addition—more room, more time, more peace.

**Get** represents intention and action. To get something means to actively pursue it, whether that's a new skill, a better job, or a helpful tool. Getting is rarely passive; it requires effort, decision-making, and sometimes risk. We get what we work for, and often what we get reflects what we've prioritized.

**Have** is the state of possession—the result of what we've removed and what we've gotten. To have something is to hold it, whether temporarily or permanently. But having is not static; it invites responsibility. What we have, we must maintain, protect, or eventually let go of again.

Together, these three words form a natural loop: we remove the old to make space, we get the new to fill that space, and we have what we've gathered until the cycle begins again. This pattern applies to material possessions, but also to habits, relationships, and even beliefs. Recognizing this cycle can help us be more intentional—choosing what to remove wisely, what to get purposefully, and what to have gratefully.

In the end, mastering this cycle isn't about accumulation or minimalism alone, but about balance: knowing when to let go, when to pursue, and when to simply appreciate what we already hold.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about aging and the milestones of adult life, interspersed with a recurring image of listening for something magical that never answers back.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Room

Somewhere around thirty, the walls of the house started breathing. Not loudly—just enough that you'd notice if you pressed your palm flat against the plaster at 3 a.m., listening for the thing you'd always listened for, the thing that lived just beneath the wallpaper of childhood and never once answered when you called.

You call it different names in different decades. At seven it was the sound in the seashell. At sixteen it was a song you almost remembered, some frequency the radio refused to tune to. At twenty-five it became the silence after job interviews, the particular quiet of waiting rooms where you sat holding a folder of your own accomplishments like a child holding a drawing up to an empty doorway.

The mortgage arrived disguised as a letter. Everyone said congratulations. You pressed your ear to the closing documents anyway, some old reflex, some hope that the fine print might hum back.

It didn't.

You get married in a room full of chairs that used to be trees. Everyone claps. Somewhere in your chest a small animal keeps its nose to a hole in the ground, waiting for whatever lives down there to surface, to say *yes, this is it, this is the proof*. The animal has been waiting since you were small enough to fit inside a coat closet and believe the coats were listening back.

Then children, maybe. Or the absence shaped exactly like children. Either way, the house grows a new room nobody remembers building. You put your ear to its door before bed. Nothing. Just your own pulse, patient as weather.

Forty arrives like a library that's quietly rearranged itself while you were reading. The books you loved are still there but the shelf numbers have changed. You walk the aisles anyway, trailing a finger along the spines, listening for the spine that will crack open on its own and read itself to you in a voice you half-recognize as belonging to someone you used to be, or might have been, or dreamed once in a fever.

Your parents become smaller. This is not metaphor. You watch them fold into their recliners like paper cranes losing their crease, and you sit beside them in the evenings, both of you facing the television, both of you—you realize suddenly—still listening. Still tilting your heads very slightly toward the window, the hallway, the space behind the furnace, as if the house might finally cough up whatever it's been swallowing since 1987.

The grandchildren, if they come, ask you what you're doing when you go quiet like that, head cocked, eyes unfocused.

*Listening,* you tell them.

*For what?*

You don't have an answer that fits in a sentence. It's the thing under the bed that was never a monster, just an emptiness with very good posture. It's the phone that rings in dreams and stops the moment you reach it. It's the last page of every book you've read twice, hoping the words might rearrange themselves into a door.

Sixty is a hallway with soft carpeting. Seventy, a room where the light behaves strangely in the afternoons, gold and slow, like it's underwater. You still press your palm to walls. You still incline your head toward closets, toward the space beneath sinks, toward the pause between one heartbeat and the next, certain—still certain, after all this—that something is in there, patient as you, waiting to answer.

It never does.

But here is the secret you'll only half-realize, near the end, in the room where the walls have stopped breathing because you finally understand they were only ever breathing with you: the listening was the answer. The tilted head, the held breath, the whole long life spent leaning toward a silence you refused to stop loving—

that was the magic.

You were inside it the entire time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental flash fiction that lists mundane rites of passage (marriage, divorce, parenthood) alongside absurd attempts to hear a hidden voice in ordinary objects.
counterfactuals.output:
**INVENTORY OF THRESHOLDS**

1. You marry him in a room that smells like folding chairs. Everyone claps at the correct moment. Later, alone in the bathroom, you press your ear to the tile and wait. Nothing. Tile says nothing it hasn't said before.

2. The toaster, if you hold it at forty-five degrees and breathe out slow, hums a frequency almost like your mother's voice saying *careful*. You test this seventeen times. You are being careful.

3. Divorce arrives like a form you didn't know you'd filled out. You initial here, here, here. In the parking lot you sit inside the car with the engine off and listen to the dashboard tick as it cools, certain — for four, five seconds — that it is trying to tell you something in Morse.

4. The refrigerator's compressor cycles on. You've read that certain motors, under stress, produce voice-like artifacts, a trick of harmonics and human hope. You stand in the kitchen at 2 a.m. in your good socks, translating hums into vowels. *Ohhh. Ahh. Oh.* Nothing conclusive.

5. A child is placed on your chest, seven pounds and furious, and you think: *this is the loudest thing that has ever not spoken to me.* You spend years listening for the sentence underneath her cries. There isn't one. There's just the cry, doing what a cry does.

6. You take up residence, briefly, inside the sound of running water. Faucet on, ear near the pipe. The pipe knocks twice, the way old pipes do, and your whole body goes electric — *is that yes, is that a code, is that her, is that him, is that God, is that the dead trying business* — but it's just the water hammer, the physics of a house settling into its own weight.

7. Second marriage, quieter this time. You stop announcing the listening. You do it in secret now: elevator between floors three and four, dryer mid-cycle, the specific groan of a screen door no one else notices. You've become fluent in silences that pretend to be sound.

8. Grandchild. You hold the phone up during the video call and swear the connection lag says something just under the words — a stutter, a syllable, a name that isn't anyone's name — before the picture catches up and everyone is laughing about something you missed.

9. At a funeral (not yours, not yet) you excuse yourself to the parking lot and lean your forehead against a vending machine, coins in hand, and listen to the compressor's low argument with itself. You feed it a dollar you don't want. It gives you a candy bar and says nothing. You eat the candy bar. It tastes like a candy bar.

10. Retirement party. Sheet cake. Someone's speech about "years of service." Later you sit with your ear against the radiator, which knocks in threes the way it has for decades, and you think: maybe the voice was never hiding *in* the objects. Maybe it was hiding in the listening. Maybe the listening was the marriage, was the divorce, was the seven-pound weight on your chest, was every threshold you crossed while pretending to look for something else.

11. You die (not yet, but eventually, the way this list has been suggesting all along) and in the last conscious hour you hear, very clearly, the machine beside your bed keeping its patient rhythm — *beep, beep, beep* — and for the first time you don't try to translate it.

You just let it be what it is:

a sound, insisting on nothing,

which is, it turns out,

the thing you'd been listening for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in list form that mixes banal adulthood tasks with fantastical, dreamlike moments, ending with the sense that some childhood magic or quest has quietly concluded.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory of a Tuesday

Buy milk.
Answer the email from the dentist.
Follow the fox with the brass key in its mouth
down the aisle where the bread should be.

Renew the car registration.
Notice the ceiling has started
whispering in a language
you almost still remember.

Pick up dry cleaning.
Step over the crack in the sidewalk
that opens, briefly, onto a sea
someone else is drowning politely in.

Pay the water bill online.
Watch the numbers rearrange themselves
into a riddle your grandmother
used to ask before bed.

Take the vitamins.
Ignore the small door in the closet,
the one with your childhood height marked beside it,
the one that used to hum.

Reply to the group chat.
Let the dragon curled in the parking garage
sleep — you don't have the hours today
to be anyone's chosen one.

Defrost something for dinner.
Feel the quiet click
of a door you didn't notice closing
somewhere behind your ribs.

Fold the laundry.
Realize the key is gone from your pocket,
has been for years,
and you cannot say when it left,
only that the lock it opened
has rusted shut, gently,
like a mouth that finally
stopped asking to be fed.

Go to bed.
Sleep, unremarkably.
Somewhere, a forest
stops waiting for you to return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness piece where the narrator catalogs their life's small achievements and losses, punctuated by failed attempts to communicate with nature or inanimate objects.
counterfactuals.output:
The kettle again this morning, that click it makes like a small bone breaking, and I said good morning to it the way I've started saying good morning to things, the radiator, the crack in the ceiling shaped like Ohio or possibly Indiana, I never learned my states properly, that's a loss, small, filed away with the others—

I told the oak tree outside my window that I got promoted once, 2009, assistant to associate, some middle rung nobody remembers climbing, and the oak did nothing, obviously, oaks are not in the business of congratulations, but I stood there anyway in my socks on the cold floor explaining tenure and healthcare benefits to bark

Won a spelling bee in fourth grade, the word was "cinnamon," I can still feel the shape of it in my mouth, that's a keeping, a small gold coin in the pocket of me, and I tried to tell my coffee mug about it, the chip on its rim like a missing tooth, mugs don't care about phonics either, everything I address is stubbornly itself

Lost my father's watch somewhere between apartments fourteen and eighteen, I've had that many addresses, that's either freedom or failure to root, I asked the doorknob in the hallway if it had opinions on rootlessness, brass doesn't opine, brass just sits there being brass, cold and certain of nothing

Learned to parallel park at thirty-one, humiliatingly late, but I did it, I did it on the first try that Tuesday and nobody was there to see so I told the neighbor's cat, who blinked and left, cats have somewhere better to be, always, that's the thing about cats

The marriage, twelve years, ended not with a door slam but with two people folding laundry in different rooms, that's a loss too big to file, I tried telling the moon about it, actually stood on the porch at 2 a.m. explaining irreconcilable, the moon just did its moon thing, indifferent white stone, no wisdom there despite what the poems promise

Baked bread once that actually rose, a small resurrection in a loaf pan, I held it up to the window like an offering, the glass reflected only my own stupid hopeful face

Buried the dog in the backyard, dug the hole myself, told the shovel thank you afterward which makes no sense, a shovel is not a mourner, but my hands needed to say something to something

The rejection letters, forty-three of them, I kept count, I told the wastebasket each time, here's another, we're friends now, we have a routine, the wastebasket accepts everything without judgment, best listener I've had in years honestly

The daughter's first steps, wobbling toward me across the kitchen tile, I called out to the ceiling like it might pass the message upward, look, look what she's doing, the ceiling stayed exactly where ceilings stay

Every small triumph, every quiet erosion, and all this talking to what cannot answer, the trees, the mugs, the moon, the shovel, the wastebasket, the doorknob, the ceiling, as if meaning might leak sideways into inanimate ears, as if the universe keeps a ledger somewhere and I'm just trying to make my entries known before the pen runs dry, before the page closes, before whatever is listening, if anything is listening, stops.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, slightly melancholic monologue about growing older, blending everyday responsibilities with strange fantastical asides, culminating in the realization that magic has left the world.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to be able to fold time like laundry—now I just fold laundry. There's a difference, though the motions look the same from across the room: the wrist-flick, the crease, the small violence of making something neat that wasn't meant to be neat. My mother could do it too, the time-folding. She kept Tuesdays in a drawer for emergencies. I don't know where mine went.

The mortgage statement arrived today wearing a paper crown, very sarcastic about it, and I paid it anyway because that's what you do when the crown insists. Somewhere between the second cup of coffee and the dentist appointment I remember I used to talk to a heron who lived in the gutter of our old house. He had opinions about my posture. He's probably dead now, or worse—retired to some coastal town, drinking gin, no longer bothering with the language of men.

I check my pulse sometimes like I'm checking a clock nobody wound properly. Forty-one beats to the dozen, or was it the other way. My knees have started speaking in a dialect only weather understands. Rain coming, they say, not unkindly, just factually, the way an old friend tells you you've put on weight.

There was a summer—I want to say I was nine, but numbers lie about themselves as much as anything else—when the whole neighborhood smelled like cut grass and something underneath it, something electric, like the air itself was considering becoming a different kind of air. We caught fireflies in jars and did not know yet that we were catching small captured stars, that the jars would end up empty by morning, that everything luminous eventually just becomes a jar.

I have a meeting at 2 p.m. about quarterly projections. I will attend it in my body, which is the only vessel I'm still permitted to travel in. There was a time you could leave through a mirror if the mirror liked you enough. Mine just shows me a man who forgot to renew something—not sure what. A library card. A prophecy. The lease on wonder.

My daughter draws dragons with the wrong number of legs and I don't correct her because I suspect she knows something I've lost the address of. She asked me yesterday if the moon gets lonely. I said probably, the way anything gets lonely when everyone stops looking up and starts looking down, at phones, at forms, at the long grey arithmetic of getting through a Wednesday.

I found a grey hair and folded it in half, out of habit, the way I fold everything now. It didn't turn into anything. It was just a hair, doubled over, apologizing for its own ordinariness.

Here's what nobody tells you: the world doesn't lose its magic all at once, in some dramatic extinguishing, some final trumpet. It leaks. Slow as a tire, slow as trust, slow as a Tuesday you can no longer find in any drawer. One day you're feeding breadcrumbs to something that might be a wish, and years later you're just feeding pigeons, and the pigeons don't even look grateful, and you don't blame them, because gratitude, too, was one of the things that leaked out first.

I'll pick up milk on the way home. I'll say something ordinary to the cashier about the weather, and my knees will have already told me the truth of it. I'll pass the gutter where the heron used to live and I won't stop, because stopping is for people who still believe something might be waiting there.

Somewhere, underneath all this—the forms, the folding, the grey conducting itself quietly through my hair like a rumor—I think the magic isn't gone so much as it's become very small and very tired, curled up somewhere warm, waiting to be asked back in. But I have a meeting. I have a mortgage. I have a daughter with dragons that have the wrong number of legs, and maybe that's the last of it, right there, small and stubborn and correct in its own way—

and I am almost, almost too busy to notice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
